teaser.text: Arch Capital Group sells financial protection when businesses, insurers or mortgage lenders face losses. Money comes in as premiums, moves through claims, expenses, reinsurance and investments, and becomes profit only when the risks were priced well.

stock.closing: The full memo explains Arch's business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: The forecast sees limited near-term upside, followed by a possible recovery. The probability-weighted price is $90.31 in October 2027, $98.28 in October 2028 and $110.49 in October 2029, equal to returns including dividends of negative 10%, negative 2% and positive 10% from today’s $100.48. Dividends do not affect those returns because every scenario assumes no dividend.

By October 2029, the bear case reaches $55.82 and the bull case reaches $214.13. That wide range reflects Arch’s cyclical earnings, discretionary buybacks and uncertain insurance claims experience. The forecast assigns 30% to the bear case, 50% to the base case and 20% to the bull case.

blocks.heading: What has to go right, and what could go wrong for Arch?

paragraphs.text: Arch offers limited near-term upside and a possible recovery, hinging on resilient earnings, disciplined underwriting and capital returns as reinsurance pricing softens. Management says its risk limits cap modeled net losses from a severe catastrophe or severe economic event at 25.0% of tangible equity, and that it will adjust its business mix as pricing changes.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Arch really make?

paragraphs.text: Cash generation was strong. Operating cash flow reached $6,172 million in 2025, about 140% of net income, while fixed-asset purchases were only $44 million. But an insurer’s main reinvestment is not machinery. It is the financial capital and investments needed to pay claims.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Arch today?

paragraphs.text: Arch looks inexpensive on reported earnings, but that first impression depends on which earnings measure is used. Reported net income includes investment gains and losses, foreign-exchange movements and transaction costs. Arch’s “after-tax operating income” removes selected items that management views as non-recurring, but it still includes catastrophes and changes in claims estimates. Forward earnings are forecasts, not accounting facts. In the second quarter of 2026, reported net income available to common shareholders was $1.047 billion, compared with $893 million of adjusted operating profit. The question is whether the adjustments and forecast describe a normal year.

blocks.heading: What has Arch guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Arch’s risk limits are boundaries, not earnings targets. Tangible equity means shareholders’ capital after goodwill and other intangible assets; a net loss is measured after Arch’s own reinsurance. A rare-event return period describes a modelled annual probability, not a disaster scheduled for a particular year. The July 2026 Florida estimate remained below the stated boundary, but the model cannot guarantee that actual losses will stay within it. The tax-rate guidance also supplies no numerical target.

blocks.heading: Did Arch keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: The performance-share plan tests whether profits build durable capital. Tangible book value per share measures common shareholders’ accounting capital after removing goodwill and other intangible assets. Arch reported tangible book value per common share of $61.71 at December 31, 2025, compared with ordinary book value of $65.11. The 2023–2025 plan targeted 11% annual growth, while the reported result was 33.65% annualized over the cycle, producing a 200% payout.

blocks.heading: What are Arch’s revenue and profit trends?

paragraphs.text: Net premiums written fell 6.9% from the same quarter of 2025, while the combined ratio worsened to 83.5%. Core earnings fell to $893 million, and net income fell to $1,057 million. Fewer shares softened the decline in diluted EPS.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Arch’s next results?

paragraphs.text: Arch is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings on October 27, 2026. The key combination is the insurance expense ratio, the amount of reinsurance business retained and the size of repurchases. A smaller premium book may show discipline, but a smaller book with stubborn costs and aggressive distributions would deserve scrutiny.
